name: Accessibility (WCAG 2.2)
description: Enforces WCAG 2.2 Level AA compliance in React and Next.js codebases. Catches the most common accessibility violations that automated tools miss — semantic HTML, keyboard navigation, screen reader support, and color contrast requirements.
author: Solon AI

rules.title: All images must have descriptive alt text
rules.description: Every and next/image component must have an alt attribute. Decorative images should use alt='' (empty string). Missing or placeholder alt text (e.g. alt='image') fails WCAG 1.1.1.

examples.good: or

rules.title: All interactive elements must be keyboard accessible
rules.description: Buttons, links, modals, dropdowns, and custom controls must be operable via keyboard alone (Tab, Enter, Space, Arrow keys). Never use onClick on non-interactive elements like <div> without also handling onKeyDown.

examples.good:
or
e.key === 'Enter' && handleClick()}>Click me

rules.title: All form inputs must have associated labels
rules.description: Every <input>, <select>, and <textarea> must have a visible <label> element or an aria-label/aria-labelledby attribute. Placeholder text alone does not count as a label.

examples.good: <label htmlFor='email'>Email address</label><input id='email' type='email' placeholder='Enter your email' />

rules.title: Use semantic HTML elements over generic divs
rules.description: Use <nav>, <main>, <header>, <footer>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, <button>, <h1>-<h6> appropriately. Generic <div> and <span> elements have no semantic meaning for assistive technologies.

rules.title: Heading levels must follow a logical hierarchy
rules.description: Headings must not skip levels (e.g., jumping from h1 to h3). Each page should have exactly one h1. Heading levels communicate document structure to screen reader users.

rules.title: Focus indicators must be visible
rules.description: Never use 'outline: none' or 'outline: 0' without providing an alternative visible focus indicator. Keyboard users rely on focus rings to know where they are on the page. WCAG 2.2 requires focus to be visible.

rules.title: ARIA roles and attributes must be used correctly
rules.description: ARIA attributes must match the element's role and state. Invalid or redundant ARIA (e.g., role='button' on a <button>) can confuse assistive technologies. When in doubt, use native HTML elements instead.

rules.title: Modals and dialogs must trap focus
rules.description: When a modal opens, focus must be moved inside it and trapped there until it closes. Tab and Shift+Tab must cycle through focusable elements within the modal only. On close, focus must return to the trigger element.

examples.bad: A custom modal that renders over the page but allows Tab to reach elements behind it.
examples.good: Use a library like @radix-ui/react-dialog or headlessui/react that handles focus trapping, or implement FocusTrap manually with a ref.

rules.title: Color must not be the only visual indicator of meaning
rules.description: Error states, success states, required fields, and other meaningful UI states must use text, icons, or patterns in addition to color. Users with color blindness cannot distinguish color alone.

examples.good: {hasError && Please enter a valid email}

rules.title: Link text must be descriptive
rules.description: Link text must describe the destination or action, not just say 'click here', 'read more', or 'here'. Screen reader users often navigate by listing all links on a page — vague text is meaningless out of context.

examples.good: Read more about our deployment strategy

rules.title: Dynamic content updates must use ARIA live regions
rules.description: When content updates without a page reload (toast notifications, form errors, loading states, search results), use aria-live='polite' or aria-live='assertive' so screen readers announce the change.
